35 In the circuits shown, the power supply has an electromotive force (e.m.f.) greater than the
normal operating voltage of the lamp. The internal resistance of the power supply is negligible.
The resistance of the variable resistor is adjusted from zero to its maximum value.
In which circuit could the voltage across the lamp change from zero to its normal operating
voltage and not exceed its normal operating voltage?
A
B
C
D

hints: Notice the e.m.f. is greater than the normal lamp voltage, so the lamp must never be connected directly across the supply when the variable resistor is at zero.
Check what happens in each circuit when the variable resistance is zero: does the lamp get shorted to $0 \text{ V}$ or does it get the full e.m.f.?
For the circuit that starts at $0 \text{ V}$, think how a fixed series resistor and a parallel variable resistor form a potential divider that can limit the maximum lamp voltage to below the e.m.f.
walkthrough: Identify the requirement: $V_{lamp}=0$ at one end of the adjustment and $V_{lamp}=V_{normal} < E$ at the other end, never $V_{lamp}=E$.

Test zero resistance: in C the series variable at zero leaves the lamp across $E$; in A the series variable at zero leaves the lamp parallel combination across $E$; in D the lamp is always across $E$. All three give $V_{lamp}=E$ and would exceed normal voltage.
In B the lamp is in parallel with the variable resistor, and this combination is in series with a fixed resistor. When $R_{variable}=0$ the lamp is shorted, so $V_{lamp}=0$.
As $R_{variable}$ is increased, more of the total resistance is in parallel with the lamp, so by the potential divider rule $V_{lamp}=E \times R_{parallel}/(R_{fixed}+R_{parallel})$ increases.
With a suitable $R_{fixed}$ and maximum $R_{variable}$, the divider can be arranged so the maximum $V_{lamp}$ equals $V_{normal}$ and never reaches $E$. This is option B.

A.explanation: When the variable resistor is zero the parallel lamp and fixed resistor are directly across the e.m.f., so the lamp voltage equals the e.m.f. which is greater than its normal voltage.

B.explanation: With the variable resistor at zero the lamp is short-circuited to $0 \text{ V}$, and at maximum resistance the fixed series resistor drops the excess e.m.f. so the lamp can reach only its normal voltage.

C.explanation: When the variable resistor is zero the lamp alone is across the supply, so the lamp voltage equals the e.m.f. and exceeds its normal operating voltage.

D.explanation: The lamp is always directly across the supply, so its voltage is always the e.m.f. and cannot be reduced to zero by the parallel variable resistor.
